_comment: The pipeline's error budget, as an arithmetic constraint rather than an intention.
End-to-end success across m independent stages is p^m. The constants are
unforgiving and the intuition is wrong: at 99% per stage, ten stages reach 90.4%
and a hundred reach 36.6%; at 85% per stage, ten stages reach roughly 20%.
Measured behaviour is worse still — in a seven-model comparison on stepwise
reasoning, one model scored 100% at four steps and 0% at five, and at 11-12 steps
every model tested scored 0%.
That measurement is of an UNVALIDATED autoregressive chain, which is not what this
pipeline is: each stage boundary carries a typed contract, a gate set, and a
persisted revision, and the compiled-graph literature reports that pre-validated
typed execution beats free-form chaining on both accuracy and cost. So depth is
affordable here — but only in proportion to per-stage reliability, and that is the
trade this file makes explicit.
`npm run check:depth` fails when per_stage_floor^depth < end_to_end_target. Adding
a twelfth stage therefore forces one of three visible decisions: raise the floor,
lower the target, or do not add the stage. None of them can be made silently.
Neither number is measured yet. They are declared targets, and the evaluation
pipeline (ADR-0008) is what will replace them with observations. Until then this
check constrains the design, not the system.
`max_feedback_rounds` bounds the reflexive loop ADR-0008 adds to Pipeline A: a gate
FAIL routes back to `refine`, which then re-runs `lint`. Every round is therefore TWO
more stage executions against the same budget, and the cap is derived from that rather
than chosen: 11 stages at the 99.5% floor reach 94.64%, three rounds add six executions
for 17 total and 91.84%, and a fourth would reach 19 for 90.93% -- still inside target,
but the headroom left for a twelfth STAGE would be gone. check:depth enforces the
worst case, so raising this cap fails the build unless the floor or the target moves.
